column21: One mole of solute against about 55 moles of water puts the fraction near $1/56 \approx 0.018$, and a mole fraction cannot exceed 1, which also rules out the printed 1.770 without any arithmetic.
column23: wrong_exponent: A student dividing 1 by 56.5 by hand and setting the first digit one column too early gets 0.177 instead of 0.0177 - the key's digits with the point one place right. The solute is 1 mole against $1000/18 = 55.5$ moles of water, so the fraction is 0.0177. || wrong_exponent: The same long division slipped two places gives 1.770, the key's digits with the point moved twice. A mole fraction is a part of a whole and cannot exceed 1, so this one is out on its face, before $1/(1+55.5)$ is worked out.
column25: This question requires a molality to be converted into a mole fraction, demonstrated by the stem's "1.00 m aqueous solution" supplying the solvent only as a mass.

column23: true_statement_trap: A student who carries the $3n$ endosperm of double fertilisation as the rule reads "Haploid endosperm" as the error planted in the set. In a lizard the septum is incomplete and the two streams still meet in the ventricle.
column25: This question requires the class-level circulation pattern to be recalled for the animals named, demonstrated by the stem's "two separate circulatory pathways" and four animals drawn from four different vertebrate classes.

column23: condition_ignored: Over most of the ocean the animals grazing phytoplankton are primary consumers, so a student answering for the ocean generally reaches for that level. The stem's condition is "deep": the aphotic zone grows no producers, so nothing living there can graze one. || true_but_out_of_scope: The animals the deep sea is known for are predators with outsized jaws, so a student picturing an anglerfish puts the fauna at the end of the chain. column11: Sulphur has a gaseous phase as well as a sedimentary reservoir, so the option that files it as gaseous is defensible on a partial reading of the cycle.
column21: Carbon's reservoir is the atmosphere, so carbon cannot head a sedimentary list; that one fact strikes out option 1 and option 4, which both put carbon under 'Sedimentary nutrient cycle'.
column23: semantic_reversal: Sulphur travels through the air as $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2S}$, so a student who remembers that leg of the sulphur cycle reads it as the gaseous one and the two class names change places wholesale. The class is set by where the bulk of the element is held, and for sulphur and phosphorus that is rock and sediment, so this option is the key with 'Gaseous' and 'Sedimentary' exchanged. || wrong_pairing: The nitrogen cycle is learnt as a soil story - nitrification and denitrification by soil bacteria - so a student who files it by where the bacteria work moves nitrogen to the sedimentary side and lets sulphur up into the gaseous one. Nitrogen's reservoir is the $78\%$ $\mathrm{N_2}$ of the atmosphere and sulphur's is rock, so this option swaps exactly those two elements. || wrong_pairing: Most of the Earth's carbon sits in limestone and fossil fuels, so a student who reaches for that store files carbon as sedimentary and sulphur takes the vacated gaseous place. The carbon cycle is classed as gaseous because its exchange pool is atmospheric $\mathrm{CO_2}$, so this option swaps carbon and sulphur and keeps nitrogen and phosphorus right.
column25: This question requires recall of which elements NCERT files under each of the two nutrient-cycle classes, demonstrated by the options being built from the same four elements shuffled between 'Gaseous nutrient cycle' and 'Sedimentary nutrient cycle'.

column23: wrong_site_or_stage: Rods do outnumber cones across the retina as a whole, by roughly twenty to one, so a student who stored that overall ratio applies it here. The ratio inverts at the fovea, which is the one patch of retina with cones and no rods. || wrong_site_or_stage: The optic nerve leaving the eye is a real retinal landmark, and a student who remembers that the back of the retina has one named special spot takes the fovea for it. That spot is the optic disc, the blind spot, which lies beside the fovea and has no photoreceptors at all. || semantic_reversal: A student who remembers that the fovea holds only one kind of photoreceptor but not which kind names rods, since rods are the retina's majority receptor. The key's "has no rods" is turned into "Only rods are present", which is the same fact with the two receptors exchanged.
column25: This question requires one stored fact about what the fovea is made of, demonstrated by option 2's "High density of cones occur, but has no rods", against which each of the other three sets a different true retinal fact at the fovea.

column23: true_statement_trap: The general description of a fungus is a filamentous, multicellular body, so "unicellular" reads like the planted error to a student checking statements against that rule. Yeast is the textbook exception to it, so the statement is true and the stem's "wrong" is not satisfied. || true_statement_trap: A student who holds Penicillium only as "the green mould that gave us penicillin" and files all moulds with yeast reads "multicellular" as the error. Penicillium's mycelium is septate and multicellular, so both halves of the statement hold and it is not the wrong one. || true_statement_trap: Drosophila and E. coli are the genetics organisms a student can name, so an attribution to Neurospora reads like an invention. Beadle and Tatum's one-gene-one-enzyme work was done in Neurospora, so the statement is true and fails the stem's negation.
column25: This question requires four stored facts about named fungi checked one at a time, demonstrated by the stem's "Choose the wrong statement:" over four options that share no subject matter beyond being fungi, "Morels and truffles are poisonous mushrooms" among them.

column11: The stem does not say whether the grandson comes through a son or a daughter, and the two readings give two different offered values (counting only daughters' sons versus all grandsons), so a trap option is the exact result of the other reading.
column23: calculation_slip: A student who treats the sex of the grandchild as still open multiplies the $\frac{1}{2}$ that a carrier daughter passes on the allele by a further $\frac{1}{2}$ for the child being a boy, and gets $0.25$. The stem has already fixed the grandchild as a grandson, so that second factor has been spent. || calculation_slip: The colour blind father has one $X$ and gives it to every daughter, and a student who carries that all-or-none transmission into the next generation has the carrier daughter passing the allele to all her sons, which gives $1$. She has two $X$ chromosomes and only one carries the allele, so half her sons receive it and the figure is $0.5$.
column24: X-linked recessive inheritance: an affected father makes every daughter a carrier
column25: This question requires a probability chained across two generations, demonstrated by the stem's "probability of their grandson being colour blind", which cannot be written until the daughters' genotypes are fixed from the father's.
column26: X-linked recessive inheritance: an affected father makes every daughter a carrier
column27: Trace the father's X^c to his daughters, who are all carriers, then apply segregation at that carrier's X pair to her sons to get the chance the grandson is affected.
column28: law of segregation; probabilities along a pedigree path multiply
column37: It is a sex-linked recessive disorder due to defect in either red or green cone of eye resulting in failure to discriminate between red and green colour. || This defect is due to mutation in certain genes present in the X chromosome. || Males have only one X chromosome and females have two. || The mother is not herself colour blind because the gene is recessive. || The son of a woman who carries the gene has a 50 per cent chance of being colour blind.

column23: semantic_reversal: A student who holds that something about the implantation is wrong, but not what, keeps implantation in its normal place and moves the fault onto the embryo. The site clause is inverted: the key reads "at site other than uterus" and this option reads "in the uterus", which is where implantation is supposed to happen. || other_one_fact: An ectopic pregnancy does have to be ended, so a student who remembers the outcome rather than the word reaches for the option about a pregnancy being terminated. A pregnancy lost to hormonal failure is a different event in the same family; "ectopic" names where the embryo implanted, not how the pregnancy finished. || no_derivation_route: Nothing in the word "ectopic" or in the account of the condition touches the embryo's genotype, and the genetic claim also appears inside option 4, where it is at least paired with a site. The reaches that do land on printed options are the pregnancy's ending in option 1 and keeping the uterus as the site in option 4, so no route selects this one on its own.
column25: This question requires the strict reading of one definition, demonstrated by option 3's "Implantation of embryo at site other than uterus", which fixes the term on the site rather than on the embryo.

column23: neighbouring_fact: A student whose one rule about prokaryotes is that they are stripped-down cells lacking what a plant cell has reaches for the cyanobacterium in the list. What prokaryotes lack is a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; Nostoc has a rigid wall outside its membrane, with a mucilaginous sheath over that. || neighbouring_fact: A fungal wall is chitin rather than cellulose, so a student who reads "cell wall" as the cellulose wall of a plant cell concludes the mould has none. Aspergillus does have a wall; the material is different, not missing. || no_derivation_route: The reaches that land on printed options are prokaryotic simplicity in option 1 and "cell wall" read as cellulose only in option 2. Neither reaches Funaria: it is a green plant whose wall is the cellulose one those routes are built around, so no half-held rule leaves a moss wall-less.
column25: This question requires one diagnostic feature of a named microorganism, demonstrated by option 4's "Mycoplasma", the group whose cells are bounded by a membrane alone.

column23: scientist_swap: Sutton is the name a student reaches for whenever the question is about genes sitting on chromosomes, because the chromosomal theory of inheritance is his. Linkage was named by Morgan, from crosses in which two genes on one chromosome failed to assort independently. || scientist_swap: Boveri's name is printed beside Sutton's in the chromosomal theory, so a student who stores the pair as one unit and reaches for the chromosome work can land on either half of it. Neither of them coined linkage; the term came out of Morgan's fly-room crosses. || scientist_swap: Linkage is taught as the exception to independent assortment, so a student who reaches for the author of the law rather than the author of the exception picks Mendel. Mendel's pea genes did assort independently; Morgan named the case where they do not.
column25: This question requires one attribution, demonstrated by the stem's "The term ''linkage'' was coined by" and option 2's "T.H. Morgan".
column37: Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome

column23: other_one_fact: A student who remembers that the molar count changes between the two sets - two milk molars against three permanent molars per half jaw - reaches for Molars as the type the milk set lacks. Molars sit in both sets; the premolars are what the permanent set adds, erupting in the places the milk molars vacate.
column25: This question requires one stored dental formula to be read for a missing tooth type, demonstrated by the stem "The primary dentition in human differs from permanent dentition in not having one of the following type of teeth".

column23: other_one_fact: Dinoflagellates are the other protist group taught with a reinforced wall - stiff cellulose plates set in the surface - so a student holding "the protists with armoured walls" reaches for them. Their plates are many and fixed in place; the two thin shells that fit over each other are the diatom's silica frustule.
column25: This question requires one diagnostic group feature to be recalled, demonstrated by the stem "the cells walls form two thin overlapping shells which fit together".

column23: look_alike_term: A student who keeps the textbook description - the molecule that carries the gene into the host - reaches for the plain word for a thing that carries, and vector and carrier are the paired transport words from disease transmission. Carrier names an organism harbouring a pathogen; no DNA molecule is called one. || fabricated_term: Transformation is the chapter's name for getting recombinant DNA into a host, so a student who recalls that step builds the agent noun from it. The word the chapter forms is transformation, the process; nothing in it is called a transformer. || true_but_out_of_scope: Template is the DNA-with-a-job term a student already owns - the strand a polymerase copies - and the gene of interest is indeed copied during cloning. Template names the strand that is read to build a new strand; the question asks for the molecule the gene is integrated into.
column25: This question requires one term to be supplied from its definition, demonstrated by the stem "The DNA molecules to which the gene of interest is integrated for cloning is called".

column23: wrong_quantity: Three is the right count for the cells of the mature pollen grain, so a student who stored "three-celled" without storing which cells answers three sperms. The three are two sperms and one vegetative cell, so the sperm count is two. || intermediate_value: A student who remembers that pollen is shed at the two-celled stage - one vegetative cell and one generative cell - reads the generative cell as the sperm and stops there. The generative cell is not yet a gamete: it divides to give the two sperms, which is why the mature male gametophyte holds three cells. || semantic_reversal: A student who keeps the two-to-one ratio but not which cell type is the doubled one lands on the reverse of the key. It is the sperms that number two and the vegetative cell that is single.
column25: This question requires both halves of the pollen grain's cell complement to be right at once, demonstrated by option 3 "Single sperm and a vegetative cell", which matches the key on the vegetative cell and fails on the sperm count.

column23: other_one_fact: The nucellus is the tissue a student is taught gets used up as the endosperm grows, so one who remembers "whatever was in there has been consumed" reaches for a degenerated nucellus. The nucellus is a solid maternal tissue; the liquid is endosperm whose nuclei divided with no walls laid down between them.
column25: This question requires one stage of endosperm development to be identified, demonstrated by the stem "Coconut water from a tender coconut is".

column23: other_one_fact: A student who remembers that endemic species are usually few and locally restricted reaches for Rare, the neighbouring label in the same set of species categories. Rare is about how many individuals there are, not where they are, and a rare species can be spread thinly over several continents. || semantic_reversal: A student who files Alien as the geography label - the species that belongs to one place and not another - lands here because the stem is entirely about where the species is and is not found. Alien reverses the words: it is found where it does not naturally occur, where endemic is found only where it does.
column25: This question requires one definition to be held apart from its neighbours, demonstrated by the stem "confined to a particular region and not found elsewhere" set against the printed rival "Rare".

column23: look_alike_term: Metagenesis and metamorphosis share the "meta-" prefix, and a student who reads that prefix as "change of form" picks the drastic change in form after the embryo. Metamorphosis changes one individual; metagenesis swaps one whole generation for the next. || other_one_fact: Polymorphism is the other term taught on the same Obelia example, so a student who remembers the example as "it has two body forms" reaches for different morphic forms. Polymorphism is about forms coexisting in one colony; metagenesis is about generations following each other.
column25: This question requires one term to be separated from two neighbours taught beside it, demonstrated by the stem "Metagenesis refers to:" against the printed options "Presence of different morphic forms" and "Occurrence of a drastic change in form during post-embryonic development".

column11: Nucleases and nucleosidases differ by one syllable and sit in two different secretions, so the discrimination is finer than the usual list recall.
column23: look_alike_term: A student who knows the nucleic-acid enzymes are the pancreatic ones meets two names a syllable apart and picks the wrong one of the pair. Nucleosidase is on the intestinal list, splitting nucleosides into sugar and base; it is nuclease that comes down with the pancreatic juice. || true_statement_trap: Maltase is the brush-border enzyme most firmly attached to intestinal juice in memory, so a student who reads the stem as "which enzyme is present" confirms it on sight and stops. The stem asks for the one enzyme that is not there. || true_statement_trap: Lipase is remembered as the fat enzyme of the small intestine, which is where succus entericus is secreted, so it reads as a confirmation rather than an exception. The task is negated, so a true membership is the wrong answer.
column25: This question requires each listed enzyme to be checked separately against one stored list, demonstrated by the stem "The enzymes that is not present in succus entericus is".

column23: other_one_fact: Stopping leakage across a tissue is the function NCERT gives the tight junction, named in the same sentence as the gap junction, so a student who kept the list of three but lost the mapping lands here. The gap junction does the opposite of sealing: it opens a channel between the two cytoplasms. || other_one_fact: Cementing neighbouring cells together is the adhering junction's entry in the same list of three, and the word junction itself suggests sticking things together, which is the reach. Gap junctions hold nothing together; they pass ions and small molecules.
column25: This question requires one of three neighbouring junctions to be matched to its function, demonstrated by the printed options "Stop substance from leaking across a tissue" and "Performing cementing to keep neighbouring cells together".

column11: The options are built so the easiest recall (yeast to ethanol) still leaves two rows standing, forcing a second genuine recall rather than elimination.
column21: (c) Trichoderma polysporum - (i) production of immunosuppressive agents appears in options 2 and 4 only, so that one pair strikes out options 1 and 3.
column23: wrong_pairing: Cyclosporin A and the statins are taught in one breath as two drugs from two fungi, so a student who holds both drug names but not which fungus carries which hangs the immunosuppressant on Monascus. Cyclosporin A comes from Trichoderma polysporum and the blood-cholesterol-lowering statins from Monascus purpureus, so this option has rows (b) and (c) exchanged and the other two right. || wrong_pairing: Cheese ripened by a mould is the case met first - Roquefort and its Penicillium - so a student reaching for the cheese row picks the one unplaced fungus here, Monascus. Swiss cheese is the bacterial case: Propionibacterium shermanii makes the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ that puts the holes in it, and once (b) is spent on cheese the statin row is pushed onto the yeast and ethanol onto the bacterium.
column25: This question requires recall of four tabulated microbe-to-product associations, demonstrated by List II being the four products printed against these organisms - 'Commercial production of ethanol', 'Production of blood-cholesterol lowering agents', 'Production of immunosuppressive agents' and 'Ripening of Swiss cheese'.

column21: Homologues must pair before they can exchange segments, so (b) has to precede (a); that one fact strikes out option 4, the only order that opens with (a).
column23: sequence_endpoint_or_adjacency: "Terminalisation of chiasmata" names the chiasmata sliding to the chromosome ends, and a student who reads it as the step that completes the exchange puts crossing over after it. The exchange is finished in pachytene, two substages before the chiasmata terminalise in diakinesis, so (a) cannot come last. || sequence_endpoint_or_adjacency: Terminalisation and the loss of the nucleolus both fall in diakinesis, so only their order within that substage is in doubt, and a student who remembers "the chiasmata terminalise just before metaphase I" puts (c) at the very end. The nucleolus is already gone by then, so (d) precedes (c). || sequence_endpoint_or_adjacency: A student with the chiasma chain right - crossing over, then chiasmata, then terminalisation - but who forgets that pairing has to come before exchange leaves (a) in front of (b). column25: This question requires one stored sequence of prophase-I substage markers, demonstrated by the stem's "Arrange the following events of meiosis in correct sequence" over four items that are each tied to a named substage - "Synapsis", "Crossing over", "Terminalisation of chaismata".

column23: semantic_reversal: Restriction enzyme and ligase are remembered as the paired enzymes of the same toolkit, and a student who kept the pair but not which one is the scissors picks the other member. Ligase runs the reversed operation, sealing two DNA ends rather than cutting one. || true_but_out_of_scope: A probe is the tool whose whole job is finding a specific sequence, so the stem's "specific locations" is the phrase that pulls a student towards it. A probe only locates the sequence by base pairing; it has no catalytic activity and cuts nothing.
column25: This question requires one tool of the recombinant DNA toolkit to be recalled by its action, demonstrated by the stem "The cutting of DNA at specific locations became possible with the discovery of".

column23: other_one_fact: Cytochromes are the haem proteins a student already ties to oxygen, since cytochrome oxidase hands electrons to it at the end of the respiratory chain, so "the iron protein that deals with oxygen" reaches for cytochrome. Cytochromes pass electrons to oxygen rather than holding free oxygen away from anything, and the nodule's oxygen scavenger is leghaemoglobin. || no_derivation_route: The only pull towards xanthophyll is that leghaemoglobin is also a pigment, and that pull cannot choose between two identically placed carotenoid options. Xanthophyll is an accessory pigment of the chloroplast, binds no oxygen and is not found in a root nodule, so no route reaches it. || no_derivation_route: The same objection read the other way round: carotene is the other member of the carotenoid pair printed here, so neither option can be singled out by the pigment reach. column25: This question requires one protective role within nitrogen fixation to be recalled, demonstrated by the stem "inactivation of nitrogenase by oxygen poisoning prevented by".

column23: other_one_fact: Urea is the nitrogenous waste a student carries over from mammals, where the liver makes it and the kidney excretes it, so "the form nitrogen travels in" reaches for urea. The cockroach is uricotelic: the waste moves in the haemolymph as potassium urate and leaves as uric acid. || other_one_fact: Ammonia is the form a student meets first - the direct product of deamination, and the waste the ammonotelic aquatic animals release - so "what the body cells hand over" reaches for it. Ammonia is the form that has to be converted because it is toxic; what these cells discharge into the haemolymph is potassium urate.
column25: This question requires one form of nitrogenous waste to be recalled at one named stage of excretion, demonstrated by the stem "discharge their nitrogenous waste in the haemolymph mainly in the Form of".

column23: wrong_site_or_stage: The filiform apparatus is remembered by what it does - guide the pollen tube - and the generative cell is the named cell a student associates with the pollen side of that event, so the feature gets moved onto the pollen grain. column25: This question requires one structure to be placed in the cell that carries it, demonstrated by the stem "Filiform apparatus is characteristic feature of".

column23: other_one_fact: A cotyledon is a seed leaf, and the coleoptile is the part a student remembers as the first leaf-like structure of the grass seedling, so the two get put together. column25: This question requires one label of the monocot grain to be supplied from its description, demonstrated by the stem "an embryo with one large, shield-shaped cotyledon".

column25: This question requires four candidate functions to be checked separately under a negated task, demonstrated by the stem "Which of the following is not a function of the skeletal system?".

column11: Ivanowski is genuinely attached to a virus discovery, so the statement is wrong only in which agent he found.
column23: true_statement_trap: This is the only option that is not an attribution, and both halves of it can be settled outright - tobacco mosaic and AIDS are both viral - so a student who reads the task as picking the statement that checks out stops at the first option. column25: This question requires four printed statements to be judged separately under a negated task, demonstrated by the stem "Select the wrong statement:".

column23: semantic_reversal: Many genes to one trait is the other way the gene-and-trait relation is taught, so a student who keeps the words one and many but not which side carries which reads this as the same claim. It is the reverse: a trait that needs a second gene is polygenic or complementary inheritance, where a pleiotropic gene has several traits following from it, as phenylketonuria brings mental retardation along with reduced hair and skin pigmentation. || look_alike_term: Pleiotropic and Pliocene carry the same pleio- / plio- sound, so a student reading the answer out of the word's root rather than its meaning is pulled to the epoch. column23: wrong_site_or_stage: Exchanging one hydrogen ion for one sodium ion is the actual pump that acidifies the filtrate, so a student who remembers the $\mathrm{Na^+}$-$\mathrm{H^+}$ antiporter by name reaches for the option that prints it. column25: This question requires deciding which of four mechanisms accounts for a granted fact, demonstrated by the stem granting that "Human urine is usually acidic" and asking only for what follows "because".

column25: This question requires each element of a triple to be assigned to the macronutrient or the micronutrient list, demonstrated by the stem "In which of the following, all three are macronutrients?"

column23: neighbouring_fact: The chemosensitive area that watches $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ sits in the medulla, so a student who remembers that the brain is where a rising $\mathrm{H^+}$ is detected reaches for the option naming the brain. What that centre does with the signal is drive ventilation up; detecting the acid is the adjacent fact, and nothing in it cuts the brain's blood supply. || wrong_site_or_stage: Bicarbonate is the blood's buffer against a falling pH, so a student who answers with the buffering response instead of with haemoglobin reaches for it. The site and the stage are both moved: plasma bicarbonate is formed in the red cell from $\mathrm{CO_2}$ by carbonic anhydrase and is trimmed by the kidney, not released by the liver. || semantic_reversal: A student who remembers that the $\mathrm{H^+}$ signal reaches a centre in the medulla and adjusts a rate takes the option that names a rate. column7: Mechanism of Muscle Contraction and Red and White Muscle Fibre
column11: Tonus, spasm and fatigue are all loosely used for sustained or failing contraction in everyday speech, so the term has to be recalled precisely rather than guessed from sense.
column23: other_one_fact: Fatigue is the state the chapter attaches to prolonged activity in a muscle, and the stem's phrase 'sustained muscle contraction' is that same picture, so a student keying on those words reaches for the sibling state. Fatigue is the fall in tension after repeated stimulation, and the stem describes tension that is held up, which is the opposite outcome. || look_alike_term: 'Tonus' and 'tetanus' differ by two letters and both name a contraction that is held, so a student storing 'held contraction' by the shape of the word picks the shorter one. Tonus is the low continuous tone of a resting muscle, kept up by motor units firing in relays, while tetanus is the maximal fused contraction that appears when the next stimulus arrives before relaxation can begin. || other_one_fact: Spasm is the everyday word for a muscle that will not let go, so the stem's 'lack of relaxation' gets answered out of clinical vocabulary. A spasm is a sudden involuntary contraction with nothing said about stimulus frequency, and the stem's 'between successive stimuli' is exactly the frequency condition that names tetanus.
column25: This question requires one term to be recovered from its definition, demonstrated by the stem 'Lack of relaxation between successive stimuli in sustained muscle contraction is known as'.

column25: This question requires four synonym pairings to be checked separately until the false one is found, demonstrated by the negated stem 'Which one of the following statements is wrong ?' with 'Eubacteria are also called false bacteria' among four 'also called' claims.

column21: Two options name their own substrates - a protease cuts protein and an RNase cuts RNA - so the stem's requirement of a DNA-cutting enzyme strikes options 1 and 3 and leaves DNase I and Hind II.
column23: other_one_fact: DNase I is the other option that really does cut DNA from the inside, so a student who reads 'restriction endonuclease' as no more than 'an enzyme that cuts DNA' finds it satisfied here. A restriction enzyme cuts only at its own recognition sequence, Hind II at a six-base one, while DNase I cuts the backbone wherever it binds, which makes it a nuclease but not a restriction enzyme.
column25: This question requires one named enzyme to be assigned to its class, demonstrated by the stem 'Which of the following is a restriction endonuclease?' with 'Hind II' printed against three general-purpose enzymes.

column23: wrong_site_or_stage: Liverworts are taught as the simplest of the land plants, so a student reasoning that the first colonist must be the most primitive plant reaches for them. Mosses need the thin soil the lichens' acids and dead crusts leave behind; lichens need no soil at all, which is why they come first. || wrong_site_or_stage: Green algae are the pioneers of the other succession taught in the same paragraph, the one that starts in water, so a student who stores 'the pioneers are algae' puts them on the rock too. column7: Excretory Waste and Structure of Excretory System in Animals
column11: The hepatic portal vein is exactly what a candidate picks on seeing 'hepatic' without checking the direction of flow, and the renal vein catches anyone who associates urea with the kidney rather than with its site of synthesis.
column23: wrong_site_or_stage: The hepatic portal vein is the vessel the chapter makes a point of, the one carrying everything absorbed from the gut to the liver, so a student who remembers the liver's special blood supply reaches for it. column23: scientist_swap: E.P. column21: Insects, birds and wind are all agents that carry pollen, and neither bryophytes nor pteridophytes produce pollen, so that one fact strikes out options 1, 2 and 4 together.

Wind carries pollen grains, which these groups do not have; the physical medium they need is water for the gametes to swim through.
column25: This question requires one diagnostic feature of two plant groups, demonstrated by option 3's "Water", the medium through which the flagellated male gametes of both groups reach the egg.

column11: Divergent evolution is the exact answer of a candidate who swaps the analogous and homologous halves of the definition pair.
column21: Shared ancestry and divergent evolution are the two halves of one account, homology, so the single fact that analogy does not run through a common ancestor strikes out options 2 and 4 together.
column23: semantic_reversal: Convergent and divergent are learned as a pair and divergence is the one the chapter spends longest on, with the pentadactyl limb, so a student reaching for the evolutionary word they can place picks divergent. The direction is reversed: divergence takes one ancestral plan to different forms, which is homology, while analogy is different ancestries arriving at the same form. || look_alike_term: Analogous and homologous differ by a few letters, and it is homologous structures that are defined by shared ancestry, so a student who mixes the two terms gives the ancestry answer. Analogous structures, like a butterfly's wing and a bird's wing, have no common ancestral structure at all; what they share is the function. || neighbouring_fact: Stabilizing selection is the one option about a form being held alike, so a student who reads analogous structures as forms kept similar reaches for it. It belongs to the adjacent topic of the three modes of selection and acts within a single population against both extremes, which says nothing about why two unrelated groups arrive at the same structure.
column25: This question requires two neighbouring terms held apart, demonstrated by the stem's "Analogous structures" and option 1's "Convergent evolution", the route by which unrelated groups come to look alike.

The same chapter requires PCR wherever the sample is too small to work with directly, which is most forensic material. || true_statement_trap: DNA-DNA hybridization is also the name of the taxonomic method for measuring how closely two species are related, so a student with the phrase filed under phylogeny reads it as belonging to another subject altogether. column7: Class – Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia
column21: Both classes are tetrapod amniotes, which settles lungs and a bony skeleton together and strikes out options 1 and 4, leaving warm-bloodedness against viviparity.
column23: true_statement_trap: Warm-blooded is the word most firmly attached to mammals, the class a student meets as the one holding its temperature constant, so a student who files homoiothermy as the mammalian character reads it as not shared and picks it under the stem's "not". Aves and Mammalia are the only two warm-blooded classes, which makes this one of the things they do share. || true_statement_trap: Bird respiration is taught as a special case, with air sacs and a one-way flow of air, so a student who remembers that birds breathe through air sacs reads lung-breathing as the mammalian half of the pair. The air sacs are accessory to lungs rather than a substitute for them: both classes breathe with lungs. || true_statement_trap: Bird bones are taught as pneumatic, hollow and air-filled to lighten the body for flight, so a student who remembers the hollow bones reads the bird skeleton as not properly ossified. A pneumatic bone is still bone, and the endoskeleton is ossified in both classes.
column25: This question requires four characters checked against two classes, demonstrated by option 2's "Viviparity", which mammals show and birds, laying shelled eggs, do not.

column11: The false option is about a direction of change over a phase, not a definition, so it cannot be checked by remembering what a hormone does - only by remembering the shape of the cycle graph.
column23: true_statement_trap: The names invite the reading that the follicle stimulating hormone does the follicle's work from start to finish, so a student who takes FSH to burst the follicle as well as grow it reads option 1 as giving LH a job that is not its own. FSH's work ends with follicular growth; ovulation is caused by the mid-cycle surge of LH. || true_statement_trap: LH is named for the corpus luteum, a structure of the ovary, so a student who files it as a female hormone reads an action on the Leydig cells of the testis as wrong. LH acts in both sexes, and in the male it was long called ICSH, interstitial cell stimulating hormone, for exactly this action. || true_statement_trap: Spermiogenesis reads like a misprint for spermatogenesis, so a student who spots the odd word takes it for the planted error and picks the option. It is the chapter's own word for the stage in which spermatids are reshaped into spermatozoa, and the sentence about FSH acting on the Sertoli cells to help it is the chapter's own sentence.

column11: Option 1 is the pair derived from tyrosine, the one amino acid whose name is routinely confused with tryptophan.
column21: Estrogen, progesterone, cortisol and cortisone are all steroids built from cholesterol, so the single fact that steroid hormones have no amino-acid precursor strikes out options 2 and 3 together.
column23: look_alike_term: Tyrosine and tryptophan differ by a syllable, and the thyroid hormones are the standard example of hormones built from an amino acid, so a student who remembers the example but not which amino acid picks them. They also pair with option 3's adrenal steroids, so neither option could be a single key; the reach that does land on a printed option is the tyrosine-for-tryptophan swap on option 1. || no_derivation_route: Cortisol and cortisone are the same objection read from the adrenal cortex: both are cholesterol-derived steroids, so no amino acid is the precursor of either. column25: This question requires one stored precursor-to-product pairing, demonstrated by option 4's "Melatonin and Serotonin", the two indoleamines synthesised from tryptophan.

column23: other_one_fact: Peptidoglycan is the wall material a student stores against microorganisms, because bacteria are the microbes whose wall the chapter names. It is the bacterial wall only, and the fungal wall is chitin - the two sit side by side as the standard contrast. || other_one_fact: Cellulose is the cell wall, full stop, for a student who stores one wall material, since the plant cell is where a wall is first taught. Cellulose walls are the plant and algal case; a fungal wall is chitin.
column25: This question requires one stored association between a group and its wall material, demonstrated by the stem's "cell wall of most fungi" against four options that are all real wall polysaccharides.

column23: look_alike_term: Polysome and polymer share the prefix, so a student who recalls only that the term begins with poly- can take the first poly- word on the list. Okazaki fragments are short pieces of DNA and no ribosome takes part in making them.
column25: This question requires a term to be produced from its definition, demonstrated by the stem describing the object in full - "A complex of ribosomes attached to single strand of RNA" - while the four options are bare terms.

column23: other_one_fact: Metameric segmentation is taught as the annelid hallmark, so a student holding it as annelid-only reads it as the feature arthropods lack. column7: Regulation of Respiration and Disorders of Respiratory System
column11: Option 2 ('inflammation of the trachea') catches a candidate who remembers only the word 'inflammation' from the definition, since the inflammation in asthma is of the bronchi and bronchioles.
column23: wrong_site_or_stage: Asthma is stored as inflammation of the airways, and the trachea is the airway a student names first, so the right event is placed one level too high. column25: This question requires the mechanism of a named disorder to be picked out from three rival mechanisms, demonstrated by the stem "Asthma may be attributed to" and each option naming a different lung mechanism, such as "Accumulation of fluid in the lung".

column11: All four statements are defensibly true as the chapter states them, yet no option covers all four, so the item cannot be closed by knowledge alone - the candidate has to guess the setter's intent among three overlapping option sets.

For example, Down’s syndrome results in the gain of extra copy of chromosome 21. || Phenylketonuria : This inborn error of metabolism is also inherited as the autosomal recessive trait. || Sickle-cell anaemia : This is an autosome linked recessive trait that can be transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are carrier for the gene (or heterozygous).

column11: The upper limit has to be found rather than read off the stem - the question never says when the process stops - and the three wrong options (a^3R/3b, a^3R/2b, a^3R/b) are exactly the values produced by the usual slips in choosing that limit or in expanding the square.

A student who integrates up to the time the charge vanishes picks up the reversed current as well and gets $a^3R/3b$, exactly twice the correct $a^3R/6b$. || calculation_slip: A student who uses $H = I^2Rt$ with the starting current $I = a$ and the duration $a/2b$ computes $a^2R \times a/2b = a^3R/2b$. The current is not constant over that interval, it falls linearly to zero, and integrating gives one third of that.
